paragraphs.context: Some time ago, I wrote a biography of George Washington.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Why the writer wanted to write this book.
paragraphs.simple: The writer once wrote a book about George Washington's life. She liked him very much, so she wanted to "visit" him again in a story.

background.note: George Washington (1732 to 1799) led the American army in the Revolutionary War. Later he was the first President of the United States.

paragraphs.context: thought it would be fun to model our cover after one of America’s most famous paintings
paragraphs.mainIdea: The cover copies a famous painting.
paragraphs.simple: The writer and the artist made the cover look like a famous painting of Washington crossing the Delaware River.

background.note: A very big painting from 1851 by Emanuel Leutze. It shows Washington standing in a boat in the icy river.
A very large art museum in New York City.

paragraphs.context: We’d like to point out several errors in Leutze’s painting
paragraphs.simple: The painting has three mistakes: a general would not stand up in a rough boat, the real boats were bigger, and the flag with thirteen stars came later.

paragraphs.context: Still, we love the painting
paragraphs.simple: Even with its mistakes, they love the painting, so they put Jack and Annie into it on the cover.

paragraphs.context: Just remember—don’t stand up in the boat!
paragraphs.mainIdea: A friendly joke to end the letter.
paragraphs.simple: The writer hopes you enjoy the trip. Her joke: do not stand up in the boat, like Washington in the painting.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the story of the magic tree house began.
paragraphs.simple: One summer day a strange tree house was suddenly in the woods near Jack and Annie's town.

background.note: Frog Creek is the small, made-up town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is Morgan le Fay's. She is a magic librarian from long ago who travels through all times and places and collects books.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic woman in the old stories about King Arthur. In these books she is a kind librarian.
Camelot is King Arthur's castle and kingdom in old British stories.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #5–8, Jack and Annie helped free Morgan from a spell.
paragraphs.mainIdea: What Jack and Annie did before.
paragraphs.simple: In earlier books they ended a spell on Morgan, answered four old riddles and became Master Librarians.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House Books #21–24, Jack and Annie have a new challenge.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A new job: four kinds of writing.
paragraphs.simple: Now they must find four special kinds of writing for Morgan's library to help save Camelot. This book is about the second one.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He looked at his clock. It was six A.M.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wakes Jack at six in the morning. She is already dressed.

paragraphs.context: Jack quickly changed into his jeans and T-shirt.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts on his clothes, puts his notebook and pencil into his bag and goes quietly out of the house.

paragraphs.context: Camelot is in trouble. To save the kingdom
paragraphs.simple: Morgan writes that Camelot is in danger. They must find four special kinds of writing for her library.

paragraphs.context: Annie picked up a piece of paper lying on the floor.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first writing: Clara Barton's rules.
paragraphs.simple: On the floor is the list of rules from the nurse Clara Barton. They got it on their trip to the Civil War in the last book.

background.note: Clara Barton (1821 to 1912) was a famous nurse in the American Civil War. Later she started the American Red Cross.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack, “and now we need to find the second thing, something to send.”
paragraphs.simple: They found "something to follow" on Sunday. Now they need the second thing: something to send.

paragraphs.context: He picked up a book lying near the note.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The new book: The Revolutionary War.
paragraphs.simple: The new book shows soldiers by a snowy river. It is about the Revolutionary War.

paragraphs.context: “We have to,” said Jack. He hated the suffering he’d seen in the Civil War.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not want another war.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hated the pain he saw in the Civil War. But they have no choice: they must help Morgan and save Camelot.

paragraphs.context: Jack shivered. The wind blew hard.
paragraphs.simple: It is so cold that Jack can see his breath. Annie tells him to pull his scarf tighter.

paragraphs.context: He was also wearing woolen pants that buttoned at the knees
paragraphs.simple: Magic changed their clothes. Jack has short wool trousers, a coat, a hat with three corners and old shoes with buckles. His bag is now leather.

background.note: A "tricorn" hat. Men in America and Europe often wore it in the 1700s.

paragraphs.context: Over 200 years ago, the United States was made up of thirteen colonies ruled by Britain.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The research book: the Revolutionary War.
paragraphs.simple: Long ago America was thirteen colonies, and Britain ruled them. From 1775 the American "patriots" fought to be free. This war was the Revolutionary War.

background.note: The thirteen British colonies on the east coast of North America. They became the first thirteen states of the USA.
Great Britain: England, Scotland and Wales. Its king ruled the American colonies.

paragraphs.context: During the Revolutionary War, British soldiers wore red uniforms.
paragraphs.simple: British soldiers wore red coats, so people called them "redcoats".

paragraphs.context: “Well, stop reading and come on,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack to stop reading. She climbs down. Jack packs his books and follows her.

paragraphs.context: When they stepped onto the ground, there were more snow flurries.
paragraphs.simple: More snow is falling. The sky is getting darker. Jack is sorry to say it is almost night, not day.

paragraphs.context: She pointed up the river. In the misty distance was a campfire.
paragraphs.simple: Far up the river, in the mist, some men sit around a fire. They all have guns.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, I think they’re soldiers,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stops Annie. The men have muskets, the guns soldiers used long ago, like in the Civil War.

paragraphs.context: Annie lifted up her long dress and ran to a tree close to the river.
paragraphs.simple: They run to a tree near the river and look out from behind it. Snow is blowing in the evening light.

paragraphs.context: In the flickering firelight, the men didn’t seem to be wearing uniforms at all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The men are poor and cold.
paragraphs.simple: The men do not wear uniforms. Their clothes are old and torn, and some have cloth around their feet instead of shoes.

paragraphs.context: But Annie took off again. She crouched behind a rock.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs again and hides behind a rock very near the fire. Jack thinks she is much too close.

paragraphs.context: “This is like hide-and-seek,” she whispered.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie thinks it is a game.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it is like a children's game. Jack tells her it is a war, not a game, and she must be serious.

paragraphs.context: But it was too late. One of the men stood up and looked around.
paragraphs.simple: Annie's voice was too loud. A man, the captain, stands up with his gun and shouts, "Who's there?"

paragraphs.context: “We weren’t spying,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they only wanted to know if the men were British soldiers or American patriots.

paragraphs.context: “We are patriots,” the captain said.
paragraphs.simple: The captain says they are patriots. Annie is very glad. The captain smiles, and his voice is kinder now.

paragraphs.context: “We’re visiting relatives nearby,” Jack said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they are visiting family near here. At the same moment Annie says they are from Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.context: “But that’s amazing!” the captain said. “My farm is in Frog Creek.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The captain is from Frog Creek too.
paragraphs.simple: The captain's farm is in Frog Creek! He asks where their farm is. Jack does not know what to say.

paragraphs.context: Just then, someone called from up the river.
paragraphs.simple: Someone shouts that it is time. The soldiers put out their fire and stand with their guns.

paragraphs.context: “Time to meet up with our commander-in-chief,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: They must go to meet the leader of the army. The captain tells Jack and Annie to go back to their family.

paragraphs.context: “It is nice to see children,” the captain said.
paragraphs.simple: The captain was writing a letter to his own son and daughter, but he did not know what to say. Annie tells him to say he misses them.

paragraphs.context: Then he turned and headed up the riverbank.
paragraphs.simple: The captain walks up the river with his men. They all go into the cold mist and Jack cannot see them.

paragraphs.context: More than anything, he wanted to go back home.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to go home. With the soldiers gone, the river feels lonely and frightening.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe we should just follow the captain and his men,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the soldiers may lead them to something to send. Jack has no better idea.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran along the riverbank. The wind whooshed over the cold water.
paragraphs.simple: They run along the river. They hear the wind, the wet snow and then many voices.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie soon came upon hundreds and hundreds of soldiers
paragraphs.simple: They find hundreds of soldiers by the river. Many carry oil lamps, and the light looks strange in the snow.

paragraphs.context: Boats like giant canoes were tied near the river.
paragraphs.simple: There are very big boats by the river. Men put horses and big guns onto them.

paragraphs.context: On Wednesday, December 25, 1776, the patriots were losing the war.
paragraphs.simple: On Christmas Day 1776, the Americans were losing. Many soldiers were tired and wanted to stop. But 2,400 of them got ready to cross the Delaware River on a secret mission, and this would change the war.

background.note: A big river in the east of the USA. It runs between Pennsylvania and New Jersey.

paragraphs.context: “Attention, troops! The commander-in-chief!” a soldier shouted.
paragraphs.simple: A soldier shouts to the others to stand and listen. The leader of the army comes.

paragraphs.context: The commander-in-chief loomed above the crowd of soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: The leader sits high above the soldiers on his horse. He looks calm and serious. Jack thinks he knows his face.

paragraphs.context: “A dangerous mission lies before you all,”
paragraphs.simple: The leader says a dangerous job is waiting for them. He wants them to be brave, and he reads the words of Thomas Paine.

background.note: Thomas Paine (1737 to 1809) was a writer who came to America from England. His writing gave the patriots hope.

paragraphs.context: ‘These are the times that try men’s souls.
paragraphs.simple: These are very hard times. Some soldiers and patriots are only brave when things are easy, and they will run away now. But people who stay now should get everyone's love and thanks.

background.note: A "summer soldier" fights only when the weather is nice and things are easy.
A "sunshine patriot" loves his country only in good, easy times.

paragraphs.context: Listening to the powerful words, Jack felt his spirits rise, too.
paragraphs.simple: The strong words make Jack feel happier and braver.

paragraphs.context: ‘The harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph,’
paragraphs.simple: When the fight is harder, the win is greater. If we get something too easily, we do not think it is very important. Things are important to us because they cost us a lot.

paragraphs.context: There was a silence, as if everyone were thinking about the words the man had read.
paragraphs.simple: Everyone is quiet for a moment. Then the soldiers cheer and clap. They are not tired now; they want to start their mission.

paragraphs.context: Of course! he thought. He’d seen that face before—on dollar bills!
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers: this face is on American paper money.

background.note: George Washington's face is on the American one-dollar bill.

paragraphs.context: “I know who the commander-in-chief is!” he exclaimed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is sure: the leader of the army is George Washington.

paragraphs.context: When General George Washington gathered his troops by the Delaware River
paragraphs.simple: Washington was the leader of the whole American army. He led it for six years, until America was free. In 1789 he became the first President of the United States.

paragraphs.context: “Hey, what are you writing?” someone asked.
paragraphs.simple: A soldier with a beard sees Jack writing. Jack quickly puts his books away and walks off.

paragraphs.context: “Find her at once and go back to your family!” the captain ordered.

paragraphs.context: “This is my letter to my children,” he said.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Send it only if they fail.

paragraphs.mainIdea: Words of courage for his children.
paragraphs.simple: The captain wrote down Washington's speech in the letter. He hopes the words will make his children brave if he dies.

paragraphs.context: This letter was the writing they’d been looking for—something to send!
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees that the letter is the second special writing: something to send. Now they can go home.

paragraphs.context: It was hard to see. The wind was blowing harder.
paragraphs.simple: The storm is getting worse. Jack cannot find Annie, and he starts to feel very afraid.

paragraphs.context: “This is George Washington’s boat,” Annie said.

paragraphs.context: “We can’t go with him,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they will only make problems for the secret mission. And they already have something to send.

paragraphs.context: But the men were working too hard to pay attention.

paragraphs.context: Just then, the boat jolted forward.
paragraphs.simple: The boat moves suddenly and Jack nearly falls. It breaks through the ice, and they go across the Delaware River.

paragraphs.context: The huge boat rocked in the water.
paragraphs.simple: The boat moves from side to side. Big pieces of ice hit it.

paragraphs.context: “Thanks a lot, Annie,” Jack whispered.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is angry: they should not go on the soldiers' secret mission. Annie thinks they can help George Washington.

paragraphs.context: Jack clung to the wooden side.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is afraid the boat will turn over.
paragraphs.simple: Jack holds the side of the boat tightly. Nobody could live in this icy water. It would be like the Titanic.

paragraphs.mainIdea: The research book: the surprise attack.

paragraphs.simple: The boat will go back for more soldiers. Jack and Annie must get out on the other side and stay there.

paragraphs.context: The wind started to pick up. The snow fell harder.

paragraphs.simple: Washington tells them to go back in the boat. The fighting is a job for him and his men.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt very grateful to George Washington and his whole army.
paragraphs.simple: The soldiers are putting their lives in danger for America's children. Jack is so thankful that he can hardly speak.

paragraphs.simple: Jack is very cold, but he does not care. He is happy because they helped Washington and helped history happen the right way.

paragraphs.context: Thunder rumbled in the snowy sky.
paragraphs.simple: There is thunder in the snowy sky, and lightning goes left and right over the woods.

paragraphs.context: He felt very confident now, after meeting George Washington.

paragraphs.simple: A bright flash lights the sky, and Jack sees the tree house high in a tall, snowy tree on their left.

paragraphs.context: Gray early light spilled into the tree house.

paragraphs.context: “The harder the conflict, the more glorious the triumph,” Jack whispered.

paragraphs.context: Long ago, the United States was made up of thirteen small colonies.
paragraphs.simple: At first many people in the colonies loved England and its king. They called England their "mother country".

paragraphs.context: Over time, though, many colonists wanted to be independent.
paragraphs.simple: Later many colonists wanted to be free from England, a country far away. These people were called patriots.

paragraphs.context: In the spring of 1775, fighting broke out between the patriots and the British
paragraphs.simple: The war started in 1775 in two towns in Massachusetts.

background.note: Two small towns near Boston. The first fights of the Revolutionary War were there on April 19, 1775.

paragraphs.context: That summer, a group of American patriots met in Philadelphia
paragraphs.simple: Patriots met in Philadelphia, started an army and made George Washington its leader.

background.note: A big city in Pennsylvania. The leaders of the patriots met there.

paragraphs.context: After the patriots won independence over eight years later
paragraphs.simple: After the Americans won, Washington left the army and went home to his big farm in Virginia.

background.note: George Washington's home and large farm in Virginia. People can visit it today.

paragraphs.context: At the beginning of the Revolutionary War, some colonists did not want to break away from England.
paragraphs.simple: Some colonists wanted to stay with England. People called them Tories.

paragraphs.context: In January 1776, a British writer named Thomas Paine wrote a powerful essay
paragraphs.simple: Thomas Paine wrote a strong piece of writing against being ruled by a king. Because of it, many Tories became patriots.

background.note: A short book by Thomas Paine from January 1776. Many thousands of people read it, and it made many of them want to be free from Britain.

paragraphs.context: Almost a year later, in December 1776, George Washington’s army was losing the war.
paragraphs.simple: When the army was losing, Paine wrote more essays called The Crisis. Washington read them to his soldiers by the Delaware River.

background.note: A group of essays by Thomas Paine. The first one, from December 1776, starts with "These are the times that try men's souls."

paragraphs.context: Paine’s words inspired the troops to continue the fight.
paragraphs.simple: Paine's words made the soldiers want to go on. They crossed the river, won the fight and gave the whole army new hope.

sentences.simple: They might die to help all American children, of the past and of the future.

parts.meaning: They were putting their lives in danger

parts.text: for all of America’s children,
parts.meaning: to help all American children,

parts.text: past and future.
parts.meaning: children from long ago and children still to come.

parts.text: about how they had helped George Washington.

sentences.simple: Annie quietly told the children that their dad would get home safely, as though her kind words could go back in time.
sentences.main: Annie whispered.

parts.text: “Your dad is going to make it home, kids.
parts.meaning: Your father will get home safely, children.

parts.text: He misses you,”
parts.meaning: He feels sad without you,

parts.text: Annie whispered,
parts.meaning: Annie said very quietly,

parts.text: as if she could send comforting words back through time.
parts.meaning: as though she could send kind words back to the past.

sentences.grammar: "Make it home" means get home safely. "As if" shows that this is only how it seems.

all aboard.meaning: "All aboard!" means "Everyone get on now!" People call it before a boat or train leaves.
all aboard.example: “All aboard!” one of the rowers called.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".

along the way.meaning: While doing something; during a trip or a time.
along the way.example: Along the way, Jack and Annie discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.

as if.meaning: In a way that makes it seem that something is true.
as if.example: He closed his eyes, as if that would make him invisible.

at a loss for words.meaning: Not able to think what to say.
at a loss for words.example: For once, Annie seemed at a loss for words.

at once.example: “Find her at once and go back to your family!”

at the same time.example: said Annie at the same time.

be about to.meaning: To be going to do something very soon.
be about to.example: They are about to set off

be in for.meaning: To be going to have something, often something bad. "We're in for a blizzard" means a blizzard is coming.
be in for.example: “I think we’re in for a blizzard,” said Washington.

be made up of.meaning: To be formed from different parts. "Was made up of thirteen colonies" means it had thirteen colonies in it.
be made up of.example: the United States was made up of thirteen colonies

be supposed to.meaning: Should do something, because someone said so or because it is the plan. "Not supposed to" means you should not.
be supposed to.example: “We’re only supposed to send it if something bad happens to the captain.

break away.meaning: To leave a group or a country and become free from it.
break away.example: some colonists did not want to break away from England.

break out.meaning: (Of a war or fighting) To start suddenly.
break out.example: fighting broke out between the patriots and the British

call off.meaning: To decide that something will not happen.

catch someone off guard.meaning: To surprise someone when they are not ready.
catch someone off guard.example: The American patriots caught them off guard.

come in peace.meaning: To come as a friend, not to fight.

come upon.meaning: To find or meet something by chance.
come upon.example: He and Annie soon came upon hundreds and hundreds of soldiers

do someone a favor.meaning: To do something kind to help someone. "Could you do me a favor?" means "Could you please help me?"
do someone a favor.example: I wonder if you could do me a favor, Jack?

ever since.example: Ever since, I’ve wanted to “visit” him again.

figure out.meaning: To understand something or find the answer by thinking.
figure out.example: But he couldn’t figure out why.

for once.meaning: This one time (it does not usually happen).
for once.example: For once, Annie seemed at a loss for words.

for the sake of.meaning: To help someone, or because someone is important to you.
for the sake of.example: For the sake of the future children of America, sir.

gentleman farmer.meaning: A rich man who owns a farm and lives on it, but does not do all the hard farm work himself.
gentleman farmer.example: the life of a gentleman farmer

get a look.meaning: To be able to see something. "Get a better look" means see it more clearly.
get a look.example: get a better look at their uniforms.

get in the way.meaning: To stop someone from doing something easily, by being where they want to go or work.
get in the way.example: Children will only get in the way.

give up.example: many were ready to give up.

had better.meaning: Should. "We better find it soon" means we should find it soon. (In friendly talk, people often leave out "had".)
had better.example: “But we better find the special writing soon.”

hide and seek.meaning: A children's game. One person closes their eyes and the others hide; then that person looks for them.

hold up.meaning: To lift something or your hands up into the air.

in and out of.meaning: Into and then out of a place again and again; between people or things.
in and out of.example: As he wove quickly in and out of the crowd

in place of.example: In place of his backpack was a leather bag.

just then.example: Just then, someone called from up the river.

light up.meaning: To fill a place with light, so that you can see it.
light up.example: until a bright flash of lightning lit up the sky.

look over your shoulder.meaning: To turn your head and look behind you.
look over your shoulder.example: When he looked over his shoulder, he was relieved.

make it.meaning: To arrive somewhere safely, or to live through a danger. "Make it home" means get home safely.
make it.example: “Your dad is going to make it home, kids.

make sure.meaning: To check, so that you are certain something is true or will happen.
make sure.example: “I just want to make sure it’s him.”

make your way.meaning: To go somewhere, often slowly or with trouble.
make your way.example: George Washington was making his way back toward them.

march on.example: You have to march on, sir!

mean to.meaning: To plan or want to do something. "We didn't mean to come" means we did not plan to come; it was a mistake.

meet up with.meaning: To come together with someone at a planned place.
meet up with.example: Time to meet up with our commander-in-chief

merry christmas.meaning: A greeting people say at Christmas (December 25).

more and more.example: They watched more and more boats land on the riverbank.

mother country.meaning: The country where you or your family first came from.
mother country.example: thought of England as their “mother country.”

move on.meaning: To go forward again after stopping.
move on.example: The boat moved on, then bumped against the shore.

no way.meaning: "No way!" means "That can't be true!" or "That can't happen!" (Friendly talk.)

nowhere in sight.meaning: Not able to be seen anywhere.
nowhere in sight.example: The bearded man was nowhere in sight.

of course.meaning: Yes, surely; you say it when something is clear now.

oh brother.meaning: "Oh, brother!" is something you say when you are a little annoyed or worried.
oh brother.example: Oh, brother, she’s way too close now, Jack thought.

on your way.meaning: Going somewhere. "On our way home" means going home.
on your way.example: “We should be on our way home now.”

out front.meaning: Outside, in front of the house.

pay attention.meaning: To watch, listen or think carefully.
pay attention.example: But the men were working too hard to pay attention.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up from a place. 2. (Of wind) To get stronger. "The wind started to pick up" means the wind started to blow harder.
pick up.example: The wind started to pick up.

point out.meaning: To tell someone about something so that they see it or know it.
point out.example: We’d like to point out several errors in Leutze’s painting

pull on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place.
put away.example: He sighed with relief and put away the captain’s letter.

put out.meaning: To make a fire stop burning.
put out.example: The soldiers quickly put out their fire.

rule over.meaning: To control a country or people and make the laws for them.
rule over.example: They did not want a faraway country to rule over them.

set off.example: They are about to set off to find the second of these

set out.meaning: To start a trip or a job.
set out.example: Now they seemed eager to set out on their mission.

soaking wet.example: They were soaking wet and covered with slush and snow.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm or brave.
take a deep breath.example: But he took a deep breath and ran to the rock.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.

take off.meaning: To leave quickly; to start moving away fast.
take off.example: They took off running across their yard.

thank goodness.meaning: "Thank goodness!" means "I am so glad!" You say it when something bad did not happen.

thanks a lot.meaning: Usually it means "thank you very much". Here Jack says it in an angry way, so it means "This is your fault!"

time and space.example: She travels through time and space, gathering books.

turn around.meaning: 1. To turn your body so that you face the other way. 2. "Turn the war around" means change it, so that the side that was losing starts to win.
turn around.example: that would turn the war around.

turn back.meaning: To go back the way you came.
turn back.example: “Should we turn back, sir?” the major said.

wide awake.meaning: Fully awake; not sleepy at all.

write down.meaning: To write something on paper so that you do not forget it.

oh man.meaning: Something you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid or happy. "Oh, man!" is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a real man.
oh man.example: “Oh, man, it is him,” said Jack.
